summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on grounds that include sex, gender and sexual orientation. The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which hears complaints of unfair discrimination, hate speech and harassment on grounds including gender identity. The Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act, signed into law in May 2024, places sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics inside a statutory hate-crime and hate-speech regime; its hate-speech offence requires a clear intention to be harmful, to incite harm or to promote hatred.

Nothing in South African law criminalises gender identity or consensual adult sexual conduct. The common-law offences of sodomy and unnatural sexual act were struck down by the Constitutional Court in 1998 in National Coalition for Gay and Lesbian Equality v Minister of Justice, applied retroactively to 27 April 1994. A residual statutory inequality kept the age of consent at 19 for homosexual acts against 16 for heterosexual acts until the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act of 2007 set a gender-neutral 16; the Constitutional Court confirmed the earlier inequality unconstitutional in Geldenhuys v NDPP in 2008, again retroactive to 1994.

Legal gender recognition is available under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act, in force since 2003, which allows a change of sex status in the population registry and identity documents and passports. The statute requires medical or surgical treatment, including hormone replacement therapy, though surgery is not obligatory; hormone therapy is available from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. The medical requirement pathologises identity and locks some applicants out, and the binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether. Reform toward self-determination is pending but not enacted. Mismatched documents expose trans people to humiliation, denial of service and, in documented accounts, threats of arrest for fraud; a 2024 Gender Dynamix report records a trans woman refused help in filing a domestic-violence case at a police station after showing her identity document, with officers mocking her. In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans for gender-neutral identification on South African identity cards, the first such move on the continent, with an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents; officials confirmed the change would take a few years as it moved through consultation toward legislation, and no enacted instrument is documented in this record.

Detention is governed by a binding precedent. On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court sitting as an Equality Court ruled for transgender inmate Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena against the Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and the Department of Correctional Services (Case 2024/070075), holding that refusing gender-affirming health care prescribed for a transgender inmate falls below the required standard of care and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. The orders compel the department to provide prescribed medical care, including gender-affirming hormone treatment at state expense, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing her gender identity, and to implement its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day. The department has had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners in place, but rights organisations have questioned whether it is implemented in practice.

Violence against visible trans women is documented. Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman, survived an unprovoked assault at a Tshwane tavern on 26 December 2024, reported on 6 January 2025, leaving her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scarring; an arrest was reported. That is the most recent documented attack on a trans person in this record, with no later instance documented. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month, a raw monthly count with no population denominator, alongside the Tshwane case. Outright International's March 2026 overview reports that violence falls disproportionately on Black lesbian, transgender and gender-nonconforming people in townships. Older documentation alleges negligent police handling of killings of gay men between 2010 and 2013, and activists and ActionAid have condemned impunity around the murder and 'corrective rape' of lesbians, including pupils.

Facility access remains contested in law. A 2024 academic analysis examines whether excluding transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms constitutes unfair discrimination under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act read with section 9 of the Constitution, and concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access. Public opinion is comparatively favourable but uneven: an ILGA survey in 2017 found 67% backing equal rights for gay and lesbian people and 72% for transgender people, while a 2017 ILGA poll found 24% of South Africans still said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals and 57% disagreed.
tangentialFactors:
South Africa ranks among the strongest performers internationally on LGBT equality indices, placing well in the 2025 Spartacus Gay Travel Index and the Equaldex LGBT Equality Index, and the official South African Tourism site publishes travel guidance aimed at gay travellers. These rankings measure legal frameworks and policy, not the township-level violence documented in the same record.

The hate-speech offence in the 2024 Act drew criticism before and after assent. Human Rights Watch and other legal experts warned the bill was vague, threatened freedom of expression and was provocatively compared to the Suppression of Communism Act of 1950; the wording was tightened after 2016 public consultation to require a clear intention to harm, incite harm or promote hatred. The Department of Justice's National Task Team, established in 2011, and the National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities of April 2014 addressed sex- and gender-based violence with a rapid response team for unsolved cases, and Justice Minister Jeff Radebe earlier launched a government programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence citing the Constitution's equality clause. These are policy instruments, and this record contains no evidence of their operational results.

Access to gender-affirming care in the public system is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital in December 2024 over year-long delays in treatment. Private care is concentrated in the major cities, and public-system waiting lists force rural patients to travel for treatment. A trans visitor who needs a prescription refill should expect the public route to be slow and the private route to be urban and paid.

Public opinion data in this record is dated. The Progressive Prudes study of 2015 found 55% would accept a gay family member and 51% that gay people should have the same human rights; Afrobarometer in 2016 placed South Africa second in Africa at 67% comfortable with a same-sex couple next door against a 21% Africa-wide average; the ILGA figures above are from 2017; an Ipsos poll in May 2021 found 71% supporting some legal recognition for same-sex couples, with 18% having attended a same-sex wedding. None of these measures current attitudes toward transgender people specifically.

Court decisions extending protections to same-sex couples before and after the Civil Union Act of 2006 cover immigration benefits, employment and pension benefits and joint adoption. The Civil Union Act has been in force since 2006.
localsOnly:
Gender-affirming care for minors is available under the statutory pathway: hormone therapy from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. Provision is split between a small private sector concentrated in the cities and a public system with long waits, so young people outside the metros travel to major centres for treatment.

Conversion therapy is not prohibited under the Children's Act 38 of 2005. A bill introduced in 2021 would ban it on children; it is not documented as enacted in this record. The push followed the deaths of three teenagers aged 15 to 19 at a conversion therapy camp whose operators were convicted of murder and child abuse in February 2015.

The Department of Correctional Services maintains a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners. The November 2025 Equality Court orders in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre require the department to enforce that procedure, provide prescribed medical care at state expense and permit clothing and cosmetics expressing a detainee's gender identity.

Legal gender recognition requires satisfying medical requirements under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act, and the cost and delay of doing so is itself a barrier documented by campaigners writing in June 2025 and January 2026. Non-binary people cannot be recognised at all under the binary classification; a non-binary teenager, Zade de Kock, petitioned the Department of Home Affairs over being required to carry inaccurate gender markers throughout his schooling.

South Africa has no specific anti-bullying statute. The Protection from Harassment Act 17 of 2011 and the Child Justice Act 75 of 2008 are the instruments used for homophobic harassment and youth offenders. Department of Basic Education figures cited in this record show very high general bullying rates: a 2015 TIMSS survey found 44% of Grade 5 pupils bullied weekly and 34% monthly, the highest of 38 countries, with Grade 9 pupils third-most bullied at 17% weekly and 47% monthly. These figures are not broken down by gender identity.

LGBT student organisations operate at the universities of the Witwatersrand and Cape Town, Stellenbosch, Johannesburg and the Western Cape. Pride events are held annually in Cape Town, Johannesburg, Durban, Pretoria and Soweto, with smaller events in Bloemfontein, Polokwane, Gqeberha, Mbombela, East London, Pietermaritzburg and Knysna; the first Lesbian and Gay Pride march in Johannesburg on 13 October 1990 drew about 800 people.
outOfScopeNotes:
No provision on border checks, entry screening or security screening of travellers appears in this inventory. Whether document markers, gender presentation or binders and prosthetics trigger secondary screening at South African ports of entry is unresolved and not sourced here.

No trans-specific killing rate with a denominator is available. The only quantified violence figure is OUT LGBT Well-being's count of five LGBTQIA+ murders in December 2024, a raw monthly count covering the whole LGBTQIA+ population with no population base and no comparison to South Africa's general homicide rate, so it cannot be read as a trans-specific rate or ranked against other jurisdictions.

Whether the Equality Court's facility-access reasoning extends to visitors using gendered bathrooms, changing rooms and security queues is unresolved. The 2024 academic article argues the law as applied does not deliver equal protection, but no court ruling on the point is in this record.

The status of the gender-neutral identity card announced in October 2021 is unresolved: this inventory documents the announcement and an official statement that implementation would take a few years through consultation to legislation, but no enacted instrument. The status of the 2021 conversion-therapy bill is likewise unresolved beyond it not being documented as law.

Public-opinion and equality-index figures date from 2015 to 2026 and measure different populations and categories; none is a current measure of attitudes toward transgender people specifically. The 2017 ILGA figures are historical.
